title: The goddess who is Vishnu's sleep
hook: the first story: Vishnu asleep on the waters, two demons rising, and Brahma praising the goddess who is Vishnu's sleep
carry: the goddess's power moves even the gods

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Devi Mahatmya opened in a forest: two worried men, and the goddess who binds the mind, and frees it.
screen: `THE DEVI MAHATMYA.` · `TWO MEN IN A FOREST.`

segments.voice: No land. Only water, everywhere, at the end of an age. On it Vishnu lies asleep on the great serpent. From his navel grows a lotus, and on it sits Brahma, the creator. Then, out of the dirt in Vishnu's ears, two demons are born: Madhu and Kaitabha. They see Brahma on his flower and decide to kill him. Brahma looks down at Vishnu, the one who could protect him. Vishnu doesn't move. This is the sage Medhas's first story, and the goddess is in it from the start, though not where you'd look.
screen: `ONLY WATER, AT THE END OF AN AGE.` → `TWO DEMONS RISE.` → `VISHNU WON'T WAKE.`

segments.voice: Brahma doesn't shake Vishnu or call his name. He turns to the sleep itself. Here Vishnu's sleep has a name, Yoganidra, and she is the goddess. So Brahma praises her. In paraphrase: you hold up this world, create it, protect it, and at the end take it back. You are the great knowledge and the great illusion, the dark night at the end of things, and beauty, modesty and understanding. Who could praise you enough, when you put even Vishnu to sleep? Then a request: wake him, and confuse these two demons. The goddess answers, drawing out of Vishnu's eyes, mouth, nostrils, arms, heart and chest. Vishnu wakes and fights them for a very long time. Then the strangest moment. Confused by the great illusion and proud of their strength, the demons tell Vishnu they're pleased with him: ask us a boon. He asks: be killable by me. Caught, they look at the water everywhere and add a condition: then kill us where the earth isn't covered with water. Vishnu lifts them onto his thigh, dry ground above the flood, and kills them there. So the goddess isn't a helper standing beside Vishnu. She's the power inside his sleeping and his waking. That's the teaching of this book, named plainly: Shakti, the goddess, is the power that moves even the gods; without her, many devotees say, even the greatest god lies still. And yesterday's confusion is at work in the demons: outwitted by their own pride.
screen: `BRAHMA PRAISES THE SLEEP ITSELF.` · `THE GODDESS LEAVES VISHNU'S EYES.` · `NO DRY LAND? HIS THIGH.` · `SHAKTI MOVES EVEN THE GODS.` · then, large: `EVEN VISHNU RESTS IN HER.`

segments.voice: Close the eyes and follow the order the text gives as the goddess leaves Vishnu: let attention wake in the eyes behind the lids, then the mouth, the nose and its breath, the arms, the heart, the chest, one place at a time, without forcing. If you pray, greet the goddess by a name your family uses, Durga, Amba, Ma; if not, let the breath be the greeting.
The Devi Mahatmya. Today, its first story: the goddess as Yoganidra, the sleep of Vishnu, who leaves him so he can wake.
Your line: the goddess's power moves even the gods. In this book, even Vishnu's sleep is Shakti. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Brahma's praise of Yoganidra in the first chapter of the Devi Mahatmya is recited as part of the whole text, and some Hindus who recite the Chandi treat the first chapter as its own opening section.

original.note: Sanskrit: yoga-nidrā, yogic sleep. In the Devi Mahatmya, the goddess as the sleep of Vishnu.

notes: Chapter 1, second half, paraphrased: Vishnu in yogic sleep on Shesha at the end of an age; Madhu and Kaitabha born from the dirt (wax) of his ears; Brahma on the navel lotus praises Yoganidra; she withdraws from Vishnu's eyes, mouth, nostrils, arms, heart and chest; the long fight; the deluded demons offer a boon; Vishnu asks that they be slain by him; they ask to be slain where the earth is not flooded; he places them on his thigh (jaghana/loins in some renderings) and beheads them with the discus. Confirm details.
The text gives a length for the fight (traditionally five thousand years); deliberately not spoken under the claims rule.
Brahma's hymn is paraphrased loosely (creating, protecting, taking back; mahāvidyā and mahāmāyā; the dark night kālarātri; beauty, modesty, understanding). Confirm it is fair.
Closing line ties the demons' delusion to the merchant's (Mahamaya at work in both); confirm a Keeper is comfortable with the comparison.
Practice reverses the text's list of places the goddess left Vishnu as a body-scan of waking; it is offered as an invitation, not as a traditional practice.
